title: Bailey v. Richardson (1950–1951)
summary: The historical decision denied trial safeguards in a loyalty dismissal on the premise that government office was outside due-process protection.

sections.Parties: Bailey, a training officer at the Federal Security Agency, challenged her dismissal following Civil Service Commission loyalty review.
sections.Material Facts: The Loyalty Review Board found reasonable grounds to regard her as disloyal. She could present written and oral defenses through counsel, but received neither informants’ identities nor dates and places of the alleged organizational activity, and could not confront or cross-examine the informants.
sections.Procedural History: The D.C. Circuit rejected her procedural challenge. An equally divided Supreme Court affirmed, so the note does not attribute a reasoned Supreme Court majority opinion to that disposition.
sections.Issue: Did the Due Process Clause require specific charges, open evidence, confrontation, and cross-examination before the government dismissed Bailey on loyalty grounds?
sections.Holding: The court of appeals denied those protections because it viewed government office as outside the Due Process Clause’s protection; the equally divided Supreme Court affirmed the judgment.
sections.Reasoning: The majority relied on the then-prevailing distinction between common-law rights and governmental privileges. The dissent emphasized the damage to reputation and employability and demanded judicial-trial safeguards. The subsequent Cafeteria Workers discussion rejects the majority’s categorical premise even while sustaining a different security exclusion.

topics.lrs-o-new-property: Bailey represents the older treatment of a government job as a privilege outside procedural due-process protection, a premise later readings reject.
